To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the belief that the identity has been subordinated to the interests of a subgroup will prompt dejection and agitation.

the first step in the process of a schism is that group members come to believe that the group has been subverted, which leads to negative emotions, which in turn decrease group identification and group entitativity.

schisms in groups are predicted by (1) the perception that group identity has been violated; (2) the subsequent negative emotional reaction; (3) the resulting low identification with and perceived cohesion of the group; (4) the subsequent low group identification; and (5) the resulting intention to leave the group.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the first step toward secession, namely, the belief that a group identity has been compromised.
the first step toward schism: the perception that a subgroup's core identity has been subordinated.

the more the group is perceived as subverting its identity, the stronger the negative emotions (dejection and agitation), the weaker the perceived group entitativy (cohesion and oneness), the weaker the group identification, and, in turn, the stronger the schismatic intentions.
schismatic intentions are a function of the interaction between group identification and negative emotions, moderated by the perceived voice.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the social psychological model of group schism is extended and refined by the inclusion of group entitativity and the moderating role of voice.
a subgroup secedes from a group because it believes that the group identity it shares with the other group members has been subverted, and it feels dejected and agitated.

the social psychological model of the schism in groups can be extended by adding the belief in subverted group identity, and the perceived ability to dissent.
